slides.title: Part 1: What Makes an Effective Team?

slides.title: What Defines an Effective Team?
text: What Defines an Effective Team?
A team is more than people working in the same room.
▪ Definition:A small group with complementary skills committed to a common purpose — holding themselves and each other accountable
Four Key Characteristics
▪ Deliverables:Both individual results AND collective work products — the team produces what no single member could alone
▪ Skills:Complementary abilities with mutual accountability — technical, problem-solving, and interpersonal
▪ Purpose:Committed to common goals and a shared approach to achieving them
▪ Leadership:Shared responsibility among members — not concentrated in one person
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 5

slides.title: Why Teams Matter
text: Why Teams Matter
Teams consistently outperform individuals on complex, interdependent tasks.
Enhanced Performance
▪ Teams outperform individuals on complex, interdependent tasks
▪ Cross-functional teams reduce handoffs and coordination overhead
▪ Diverse skills enable creative problem-solving impossible for a single person
Organisational Benefits
▪ Flexibility:Teams can be formed, disbanded, or maintained as project needs change
▪ Efficiency:Coordinated effort achieves more results in less time
▪ Innovation:Diverse skill sets combine to solve problems in novel ways
▪ Teams build individual careers by developing communication, leadership, and collaboration skills
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 5

slides.title: Part 2: Effective Team Structure and Value
text: Part 2: Effective Team Structure and Value
Size, skills, commitment, approach, and accountability
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 5

slides.title: Team Structure — Four Key Elements
text: Team Structure — Four Key Elements
Without clear structure, even talented teams fail to reach their potential.
👥 Size & Skills
Keep teams small — easier coordination, stronger accountability.
Required skills: technical expertise, problem-solving, and interpersonal communication.
🎯 Commitment & Purpose
Shared meaningful purpose sets direction and aspirations.
Measurable milestones focus effort and small victories build momentum.
📋 Common Approach
Agree on: behavioural standards, task methodology, role clarity, decision-making process, and schedule management.
🤝 Mutual Accountability
Shared responsibility for goals AND individual clarity on personal tasks.
Peer accountability — members hold each other answerable.
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 5

slides.title: Common Approach and Standards
text: Common Approach and Standards
Teams must agree on HOW they will work, not just WHAT they will produce.
Essential Agreements
▪ Behavioural standards:How team members interact — respect norms, feedback style, meeting conduct
▪ Task methodology:Approach to completing work — which tools, review process, quality bar
▪ Role clarity:Who performs which tasks — explicitly assigned, not assumed
▪ Decision-making process:How choices are made — authority, majority vote, or consensus
▪ Schedule management:Meeting frequency, response time expectations, deadline commitments
▪ All team members must agree on these operational details BEFORE effective collaboration can begin.
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 5

slides.title: Mutual Accountability Framework
text: Mutual Accountability Framework
Accountability is what converts commitment into performance.
Accountability Components
▪ Shared responsibility:Everyone owns team goals and outcomes — not just the lead
▪ Individual clarity:Each person knows their specific responsibilities with no ambiguity
▪ Collective ownership:Team performance is everyone's business
▪ Peer accountability:Members hold each other answerable — not just reporting up
Value of Proper Structure
▪ Enhanced cooperation and reduced territorial behaviour
▪ Fewer handoffs between functions — less lost in translation
▪ Faster results through genuinely coordinated effort
▪ Organisational flexibility — teams can scale, pivot, or dissolve as needed
▪ Without clear size, skills, commitment, approach, and accountability — teams cannot reach their potential.
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 5

slides.title: Part 3: Tuckman's Team Development Theory
text: Part 3: Tuckman's Team Development Theory
Five stages every team goes through — and how to navigate them
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 5

slides.title: Tuckman's Five Stages of Team Development
text: Tuckman's Five Stages of Team Development
Bruce Tuckman (1965) — all teams progress through these stages before reaching peak performance.
Forming
Behaviour:
Cautious, polite, exploring
Focus:
Getting acquainted
Leadership:
Directive — provide clear structure and guidance
Storming
Behaviour:
Conflict, disagreement, power struggles
Focus:
Establishing roles
Leadership:
Supportive coaching — facilitate conflict resolution
Norming
Behaviour:
Cooperating, establishing standards
Focus:
Process definition
Leadership:
Collaborative facilitation — help establish norms
Performing
Behaviour:
Collaborative, anticipating needs
Focus:
Goal achievement
Leadership:
Delegative oversight — empower and step back
Adjourning
Behaviour:
Reflecting, separating
Focus:
Closure & evaluation
Leadership:
Reflective leadership — celebrate and evaluate
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 5

slides.title: Applying Tuckman's Model in Practice
text: Applying Tuckman's Model in Practice
Use the model as a diagnostic tool — not just a framework to memorise.
▪ Diagnose your stage: Honestly assess where your team is right now based on actual behaviour — not intentions
▪ Set realistic expectations: Development takes time; don't expect Performing-level output in Forming
▪ Plan targeted interventions: Stuck in Storming? Run a structured values discussion. Missing Norming? Create a team charter this week.
▪ Normalise conflict: Storming is development, not failure — suppressing it delays rather than prevents the issues
▪ Monitor for regression: Membership changes, scope shifts, or stress can send a Performing team back to Storming
▪ Build psychological safety: Teams can't reach peak performance unless members feel safe to speak up, fail, and challenge ideas
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 5

slides.title: Leadership Strategies by Stage
text: Leadership Strategies by Stage
Match your leadership style to what the team actually needs right now.
▪ Forming — Directive: Provide clear structure and guidance; define goals, roles, and expectations explicitly
▪ Storming — Coaching: Facilitate conflict resolution; acknowledge tension, separate people from problems
▪ Norming — Collaborative: Help establish shared processes and norms; encourage team ownership of decisions
▪ Performing — Delegative: Empower the team; step back from task direction and focus on removing obstacles
▪ Adjourning — Reflective: Celebrate achievements; run genuine retrospectives; capture lessons for future teams
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 5

slides.title: Tuckman in Practice — Challenges & Critical Elements
text: Tuckman in Practice — Challenges & Critical Elements
Understanding why teams stall — and what to address to move forward.
The Three Critical Elements
For teams to become productive, all three must be addressed:
📄 Content — What the team does — tasks and goals
⚙️ Process — How the team works — methods and procedures
💬 Feelings — How team members relate to each other
⚠️ Problem: Most teams focus only on Content, neglecting Process and Feelings — explaining why technically strong teams often underperform.
Common Team Challenges
▸ Many teams get stuck in Storming — accept conflict as normal and never move forward
▸ Some never progress beyond Forming — lack of clear direction or leadership
▸ Incomplete Norming leads to regression — processes not fully established
▸ Teams only reach full effectiveness at Performing stage
▸ Timeline varies significantly — don't rush; address process AND feelings
▸ Monitor for regression during team changes or external stress
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 5

slides.title: Determine Team Roles and Responsibilities
text: Determine Team Roles and Responsibilities
Start with the project outcomes — then design the roles to match.
Process: Three Steps
▪ Step 1 — Understand:Project objectives, instructions, scope, and expected outcomes
▪ Step 2 — Identify:Required tasks and their outputs — break the project into concrete deliverables
▪ Step 3 — Create:Roles and responsibilities suited to those tasks — not generic job titles
Example Tasks for Your Project
▪ Assignment 2a:Research, critical analysis, requirements categorisation, solution brainstorming
▪ Assignment 2b:Ideation process, mockup creation, prototyping to demonstrate AI solutions
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 5

slides.title: Common IT Team Roles
text: Common IT Team Roles
Adapt the task specific to project roles— flexibility beats rigid job titles.
Team Lead
▪ Coordinates the team and ensures processes run smoothly
▪ Responsibilities:Organise requests, manage tasks, monitor workflows, host meetings
▪ In Scrum:This role is the Scrum Master
▪ Key skill:Facilitation and follow-through
Product Owner
▪ Defines requirements and ensures they are met
▪ Responsibilities:Communicates with team, provides feature guidance, sets priorities
▪ Key skill:Translating the brief into actionable tasks
Team Members
▪ Execute the actual work
▪ Dev/Design:Programmers, UX designers, software developers
▪ QA/Review:Quality assurance and testing roles
▪ Key principle: Adapt roles to your specific project needs
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 5

slides.title: Your Teamwork Process
text: Your Teamwork Process
A lightweight Agile-inspired weekly cycle keeps teams aligned without heavy overhead.
Weekly Cycle — Three Phases
▪ Planning (Weekly/Bi-weekly):Set clear deliverables; ensure all members understand goals; focus on collaboration over competition
▪ Progress Updates (1–3 days):Team lead facilitates 15-min check-ins; identify blockers; share daily/weekly plans — sync or async
▪ Progress Review (1–3 days):Product owner showcases completed work; gather feedback; adjust deliverables if needed
▪ This cycle mirrors Agile sprint ceremonies — planning, standup, and review — adapted for student project scale.
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 5

slides.title: Planning Best Practices
text: Planning Best Practices
Good planning prevents the two most common failures: unclear ownership and missed deadlines.
Purpose
▪ Ensure all team members understand project goals and deliverables before work begins
▪ Everyone should be able to state what they are doing, why it matters, and what success looks like
Expected Outcomes
▪ Clear decision:Weekly/bi-weekly work commitments confirmed by all
▪ Complete increments:Plan work that can be fully finished in the period
▪ Confidence:Everyone feels sure about their commitments
Top Tips
▪ Collaborate:Focus on team wins, not individual credit
▪ Break it down:Smaller tasks are easier to complete and check
▪ Be realistic:Factor in other assessments, work, and availability
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 5

slides.title: Foundation Elements for Effective Teams
text: Foundation Elements for Effective Teams
Seven essential components — establish these early, not after problems emerge.
▪ Select appropriate members:Match skills and personalities to project requirements
▪ Identify clear objectives:Everyone must agree on what success looks like before starting
▪ Determine roles:Assign responsibilities explicitly — avoid 'someone will do it'
▪ Hold effective meetings:Structured agendas, decisions documented, action items assigned
▪ Respect team members:Treat all contributions as valuable — diverse perspectives improve outcomes
▪ Manage conflict constructively:Address issues early before they become resentment
▪ Establish ground rules:Communication norms, response times, and meeting schedules — agree in first team
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 5

slides.title: Team Setup and Ground Rules
text: Team Setup and Ground Rules
30 minutes of setup in first meeting saves hours of confusion across the semester.
Shared Goals & Decisions
▪ Define what success looks like specifically for your team
Decision-making methods
▪ Authority-based:Leader decides after hearing input — fast, clear
▪ Majority vote:Democratic — good for lower-stakes choices
▪ Consensus:Everyone can live with it — slower but builds buy-in
▪ Average opinion:Aggregated input — useful for estimates
Communication & Meeting Norms
▪ Choose your tools:Pick ONE primary channel (Slack, Teams, WhatsApp) — don't split across multiple
▪ Set meeting cadence:Fix regular times now rather than renegotiating every week
▪ Respect and feedback:Agree on how you'll give feedback and handle disagreement
▪ Write this up as a short team charter — it becomes your reference when tensions arise.
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 5

slides.title: Your Team Process & Ground Rules
text: Your Team Process & Ground Rules
A consistent weekly cycle and shared values are what separate high-performing teams from struggling ones.
Weekly Teamwork Cycle
📅 Planning
Set deliverables, ensure everyone understands goals, focus on collaboration over competition
🔄 Progress Updates
Team lead facilitates 15-min check-ins. Identify blockers. Can be sync or async.
✅ Progress Review
Product owner showcases completed work. Gather feedback and adjust if needed.
Team Values & Ground Rules
🤔 Respond thoughtfully — consider others' views before reacting
💬 Criticise ideas, not people
🙏 Respect absent team members
📢 Communicate openly and proactively
⚖️ Manage conflict constructively — seek mediation if needed
📋 Use structured agendas and document meeting minutes
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 5

slides.title: Common Team Problems and Solutions
text: Common Team Problems and Solutions
Naming the specific behaviour makes it easier to address without feeling personal.
Individual Behaviours
▪ Ego conflicts:Competing for credit rather than contributing to team success
▪ Self vs. group interest:Optimising individual grade at the expense of team quality
▪ Poor self-awareness:Not seeing how one's communication style lands with others
▪ These usually surface in Storming — address them directly rather than hoping they resolve themselves.
Team Behaviours
▪ Defensive attitudes:Treating feedback as personal attack — fragile teams can't improve
▪ Getting off-task:Social conversation and tangents consume meeting time without advancing the work
▪ Unclear role boundaries:Two people assume someone else is handling something — nothing gets done
▪ Establishing ground rules in first meeting prevents most of these patterns from forming.
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 5

slides.title: Handling Difficult Team Behaviours
text: Handling Difficult Team Behaviours
Every team will face these — knowing how to respond is what makes the difference.
Problem
Solution
Talkative member
Use assertiveness skills — redirect with 'That's a great point, let's hear from others'
Quiet / withdrawn member
Apply good questioning techniques — use directed, open questions
Argumentative member
Use assertiveness and SBI feedback skills — focus on impact, not intent
Free rider
Set clear ground rules from the start; make individual accountability visible
Group getting lost or digressing
Use structured agendas and assertiveness to redirect: 'Let's park that and return to...'
Indecisive group
Use a facilitator; vote, use consensus, or delegate to team lead
Feuding members
Seek third-party mediation; separate content conflict from personal conflict
🚧 Common meeting traps: Hogging (talking too much) · Flogging (beating issues to death) · Frogging (topic jumping) · Bogging (getting stuck)
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 5

slides.title: Leadership in IT Teams
text: Leadership in IT Teams
Leadership is getting cooperation from others to accomplish desired goals — and it starts with you.
IT Leadership Principles
🧭 Self-organising teams — Trust individuals to make good decisions with autonomy
🔭 Clear vision — Provide direction while encouraging collaboration
🚧 Obstacle removal — Focus on clearing blockers rather than micromanaging
🌱 Learning culture — Commit to continuous improvement and evolving better ways of working
Key Leadership Qualities
🔄 Adaptability — Respond to change; listen to team input and adjust
🤝 People over Process — Prioritise relationships and human factors
🌫️ Comfort with uncertainty — Navigate complexity through collective intelligence
🪞 Be the change — Model the behaviours you want to see in your team
💬 Responsibility — Take accountability for actions and create environments where people come first
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 5

slides.title: Active Learning — Build Your Own AI Personal Study Assistant
text: Active Learning — Build Your Own AI Personal Study Assistant
30-minute activity: Individual + pairs. Use AI to solve a real problem you face RIGHT NOW as a student.
🎯 Scenario: You have 3 assignments due in the next 2 weeks, weekly readings to keep up with, and no reliable system for tracking what needs to be done — and when.
Phase 1 · Map Your Chaos (5 min)
Individually: Write down the 3 biggest friction points in managing your study workload right now.
Examples: forgetting deadlines, not knowing what to prioritise, no reminders for Moodle tasks.
Phase 2 · Design the Agent (8 min)
In pairs: Pick ONE friction point. Design an AI agent that would solve it.
Define: What is its trigger? What should it do? What should it output?
Sketch the workflow on paper first.
Phase 3 · Build & Demo (15 min)
Use one of these tools to build it:
▸ Zapier AI — automated deadline reminder
▸ ChatGPT Custom GPT — weekly study planner
▸ Copilot Studio — assignment tracker agent
Share with your peer: Compare notes, What does it do? Would you actually use it?
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 5

slides.title: Team Productivity Assessment
text: Team Productivity Assessment
How effectively do our AI-enhanced processes improve team performance and output quality?
Quantitative Indicators — What to Measure
▪ Time efficiency:Meeting duration vs. outcomes achieved; preparation time reduction with AI assistance
▪ Output metrics:Deliverable completion rates, quality scores, and revision cycles required
▪ Decision velocity:Time from problem identification to consensus and action
▪ Resource optimisation:Effective use of team expertise and available tools
▪ Track these over the semester — improvement is the goal, not a perfect score from day one.
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 5

slides.title: Team Productivity Assessment
text: Team Productivity Assessment
Qualitative assessment captures what metrics alone cannot.
Qualitative Indicators — What to Reflect On
▪ Process evolution:Evidence of iterative improvement in team workflows over time
▪ Knowledge integration:How well insights from meetings translate into actionable outcomes
▪ Collaboration quality:Balance of participation, constructive conflict resolution, shared accountability
▪ Adaptive capacity:Team's ability to modify processes based on what works — and what doesn't
▪ Run a 10-minute retrospective at the end of each project cycle: What worked? What didn't? What will we change?
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 5

slides.title: Team Productivity Assessment
text: Team Productivity Assessment
Evidence collection methods — capture evidence throughout, not just at submission.
Evidence Collection Methods
▪ Before/after comparisons:Baseline measurements at start vs. end — what changed?
▪ Team self-assessment surveys:Short pulse-checks after each sprint — track trends, not one-off snapshots
▪ Process documentation:Record modifications made and the rationale — this IS professional practice in action
▪ For FIT1055 assessments: your meeting minutes, team charter, and retrospective notes are your evidence artefacts. Keep them from your initial first meeting.
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 5
